triage.name: Epididymitis
triage.reason: Acute scrotal pain with gradual onset and urinary symptoms; key differential with testicular torsion, worked up by history, exam, urinalysis and ultrasound.

review_issues: exam: term 'Erythema of scrotum' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Most common in sexually active young men
Also occurs in older men with urinary tract obstruction or recent urinary instrumentation

risk_factors.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia or bladder outlet obstruction
Structural abnormality of the urinary tract

chief_complaints.text: My scrotum is swollen on that side

hpi.duration: Several days at presentation; often 2–7 days
hpi.progression: Starts as a dull ache behind one testicle, then worsens and spreads to the entire scrotum; urinary burning or discharge may develop
hpi.location: Unilateral, usually posterior and lateral aspect of the affected testicle
pertinent_negatives: Sudden, excruciating pain that woke the patient from sleep
Fever with red, hot skin spreading beyond the scrotum

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Sudden severe scrotal pain with vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: Prepubertal boys may have trouble localizing pain, presenting with abdominal pain, fever, or refusal to walk; epididymitis is much less common than testicular torsion in this group.
Older men more often have urinary tract infection or recent instrumentation, less often urethral discharge; pain may be less dramatic and more chronic.
May present with more severe systemic illness, atypical organisms, or abscess formation and can have less localizing scrotal findings early.

general.mild: Well-appearing, ambulatory, may walk with a slightly wide stance to avoid scrotal pressure
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, prefers to sit or lie still, may hold or support the scrotum
general.severe: Ill-appearing, flushed, diaphoretic, reluctant to move

findings.maneuver: Gently palpate the posterior and lateral aspect of the affected testicle
findings.finding: Tenderness localized to the epididymis, often with induration or fullness
Unilateral scrotal swelling with thickening of the scrotal wall
Testicular tenderness, usually less prominent than epididymal tenderness
Erythema of the scrotal skin on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Inspect the urethral meatus; ask patient to milk the urethra

findings.finding: Cremasteric reflex present on the affected side

labs.caveat: Pyuria is common but may be absent in early epididymitis or primarily epididymal infection; a normal urinalysis does not rule out epididymitis.
Positive mainly with nitrate-reducing Gram-negative bacteria; often negative in sexually transmitted epididymitis.
Leukocytosis is supportive but not required; normal white count is common in mild cases.
Useful supporting marker; higher values may indicate abscess or systemic infection.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for acute scrotal pain; rules out torsion and identifies abscess

findings.text: Increased color Doppler flow in the epididymis and testis

initial.why: Urinalysis for pyuria, nitrites, and bacteria supports urinary tract infection
Identifies causative bacteria and guides antibiotic therapy in suspected urinary tract infection

initial.test: Urine NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
initial.why: Detects common sexually transmitted causes; test of choice for gonorrhea and chlamydia
initial.only_if: sexually active young men, urethral discharge, or risk factors for STI

confirmatory.why: Confirms epididymitis and excludes testicular torsion

supporting.why: Adds to white count and suggests abscess when markedly elevated

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: No role in scrotal inflammation; ultrasound is superior for scrotal detail

decision_points: Always consider testicular torsion first; if there is sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, or absent cremasteric reflex, consult urology immediately and do not delay for labs.
Send NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia in sexually active men; treat empirically for both while results pending.
Order scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to confirm epididymitis and exclude torsion.
In older men or after recent instrumentation, focus on coliforms and obtain urine culture; adjust antibiotics based on susceptibilities.

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Most important cause of acute, severe unilateral scrotal pain and swelling in adolescents and young adults
differential.trigger: Sudden, severe scrotal pain with nausea or vomiting, high-riding testis, or absent cremasteric reflex

history: Sudden onset, often waking from sleep
Pain not improved by scrotal elevation
exam: Scrotum may be swollen but early erythema is less prominent
imaging: Absent or markedly reduced Doppler flow on scrotal ultrasound
May show 'whirlpool sign' in spermatic cord

differential.name: Fournier gangrene
differential.why_considered: Scrotal pain, swelling, and erythema with systemic toxicity can be necrotizing soft tissue infection
differential.trigger: Crepitus, skin necrosis, hemorrhagic bullae, pain out of proportion, or rapid progression with systemic illness

history: Diabetes, alcohol use, or other immunocompromised state
imaging: Subcutaneous gas on scrotal ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Testicular cancer
differential.why_considered: Unilateral scrotal mass or dull ache in a young man can be a germ cell tumor
differential.trigger: Painless testicular mass, firm nodule, or scrotal symptoms with a solid testicular lesion on ultrasound

history: Usually painless testicular mass or dull ache
labs: Tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) may be elevated
imaging: Solid hypoechoic intratesticular mass on ultrasound

differential.name: Torsion of testicular appendage
differential.why_considered: Acute scrotal pain in a prepubertal boy

history: Gradual or subacute onset over 1–2 days
Pain less severe than testicular torsion
exam: Tenderness localized to upper pole of testis
imaging: May show an avascular echogenic nodule near testis or epididymis

differential.name: Inguinal hernia
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling and pain with a groin bulge can be an incarcerated hernia
differential.trigger: Irreducible groin/scrotal bulge with pain, especially with vomiting or signs of bowel obstruction

labs: Usually normal; lactate may rise with ischemia
imaging: Ultrasound or CT shows bowel or omentum in inguinal canal

differential.name: Varicocele
differential.why_considered: Chronic scrotal discomfort or dull ache, especially left side

history: Dull ache worse with standing or exercise
exam: 'Bag of worms' above and around testis
No scrotal erythema or marked tenderness
labs: Semen analysis may show abnormal parameters if fertility concerns
imaging: Dilated pampiniform plexus veins with reflux on Valsalva

differential.name: Hydrocele
differential.why_considered: Painless scrotal swelling; may accompany epididymitis or be isolated

severity.mild: Early uncomplicated: gradual aching scrotal pain, localized epididymal tenderness, no or low-grade fever, normal vital signs, able to ambulate
severity.moderate: Established infection: marked scrotal swelling and erythema, moderate epididymal/testicular tenderness, fever, pyuria and leukocytosis, but no abscess or systemic compromise
severity.severe: Complicated: high fever, tachycardia, severe pain, possible epididymal abscess, or signs of systemic infection; may require inpatient antibiotics or drainage

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe pain with nausea/vomiting, high-riding testis, or absent cremasteric reflex
red_flags.meaning: Testicular torsion until proven otherwise; immediate urology consult and ultrasound

red_flags.finding: Crepitus, skin necrosis, hemorrhagic bullae, or pain out of proportion
red_flags.meaning: Necrotizing soft tissue infection (Fournier gangrene); emergency surgery

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or altered mental status with fever
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis; initiate resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and source control
Testicular cancer should be ruled out with ultrasound and tumor markers

red_flags.finding: No improvement after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Consider abscess, resistant organism, or alternative diagnosis; repeat imaging

complications.name: Testicular ischemia or infarction
clues: Severe pain with tense scrotal swelling
Absent or decreased Doppler flow to testicle

complications.name: Chronic scrotal pain or chronic epididymitis
clues: Persistent dull ache after resolution of acute infection

special_populations.differences: Prepubertal epididymitis is uncommon; torsion must be excluded first. Often linked to UTI or structural anomaly, may present with abdominal pain or limping. Ultrasound first.
More often due to urinary pathogens from obstruction or instrumentation; STI risk lower. May have less dramatic pain but higher risk of abscess
May present with atypical organisms, more severe systemic illness, and higher risk of abscess or Fournier gangrene; lower threshold for imaging and inpatient care.
Higher risk of complicated infection and Fournier gangrene; examine carefully for crepitus and skin necrosis.

key_questions.question: When did the pain start, and how quickly has it progressed?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1-3 days; sudden severe pain suggests testicular torsion

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain located?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral posterior/lateral aspect of the testicle, along the epididymis

key_questions.question: How severe is the pain, and can you still walk and do normal activities?
key_questions.looking_for: Moderate dull ache; severe inability to walk raises torsion or infarction

key_questions.question: Have you had any burning or pain with urination?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria suggests urinary tract infection and pyuria

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any discharge from the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Urethral discharge suggests a sexually transmitted cause

key_questions.question: Have you needed to urinate more often than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary frequency or urgency supports urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: Have you had fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever supports infection; high spiking fevers raise concern for abscess or sepsis

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting is uncommon and should raise concern for torsion

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active, and have you had a new or multiple partners recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Unprotected sex with new or multiple partners places patient at high STI risk

key_questions.question: Do you consistently use condoms?
key_questions.looking_for: Inconsistent condom use increases STI exposure

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Past STI raises probability of recurrent or persistent infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent urinary tract infection, catheterization, or cystoscopy?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent instrumentation or UTI suggests coliform bacteria rather than STI

key_questions.question: Do you have any medical problems like diabetes or prostate enlargement?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes and bladder outlet obstruction predispose to non-STI epididymitis and complications

key_questions.question: Do you take any medications, especially amiodarone?
key_questions.looking_for: Amiodarone can cause or contribute to epididymitis

key_questions.question: Sudden severe pain, vomiting, or a testicle that feels twisted or high-riding?
key_questions.looking_for: Red flags for testicular torsion requiring immediate ultrasound/urology consult

key_questions.question: Have you noticed a firm painless lump or heaviness in the testicle?
Do you have any allergies to antibiotics or other medications?

reasoning_points: Pain gradually worsening over 1-3 days, localized to the epididymis and unilateral
Associated urinary symptoms or urethral discharge suggest an infectious cause
Sexual history points to STI (chlamydia or gonorrhea) vs urinary coliforms
Red flags for torsion absent: no sudden severe pain, no vomiting, cremasteric reflex intact, no high-riding testis
Examination shows enlarged, tender epididymis without a testicular mass
Urinalysis with pyuria; NAAT positive for chlamydia or gonorrhea in the appropriate patient
Doppler ultrasound shows increased flow to the epididymis with a normal testicle
No necrotizing findings or abscess, and no evidence of testicular torsion

easy: Classic young sexually active adult with gradual unilateral scrotal pain
Tender, swollen epididymis with normal testis and intact cremasteric reflex
Pyuria and positive urine NAAT for chlamydia or gonorrhea
Doppler ultrasound shows a hyperemic epididymis
medium: Older man with recent catheterization and less clear STI risk
Mild symptoms, no urethral discharge, and a normal urinalysis
Cannot fully exclude torsion until ultrasound is performed
Subtle epididymal tenderness and mild scrotal swelling
Urinary tract infection from coliforms with a positive urine culture
hard: Prepubertal boy with abdominal pain or refusal to walk; torsion must be ruled out
Diabetic or immunocompromised patient with severe pain and possible Fournier gangrene
Normal urinalysis and NAAT but ultrasound supports epididymitis
Recurrent or chronic epididymitis with no clear infectious source
